Pecos River basin · SWAT+ rev 62 with gwflow · experiment ledger

Where the flow is wrong, and what has moved it

Every panel below is computed from finished model runs and USGS daily flow, in real units (m³/s, mm). The model is not calibrated yet. One cause of the large over-prediction has been found and fixed (rain-gauge gaps). The remainder was traced to specific tributaries, oversized channel widths and missing diversions, and a groundwater-routing defect whose patch (v24) raised flows instead of lowering them. Tests of the missing processes (v31/v32) cut Brantley from 9.5 to 4.1 m³/s (observed 2.35); the recommended base is v32a. The model has been extended to 2025 (v30_ext, finished 2000-2025). Use the controls to compare runs.

Groundwater: model against observation wells

Annual mean water-table elevation (m above sea level) at the 70 USGS/TWDB observation wells, against the value simulated in the 2 km gwflow cell that contains each well. Choose any finished run: long runs (v25, v30ext) cover the years when most wells were measured (after 2008); the 4-year runs cover 2000–2003 only, so they have few observations.

Observed against simulated head, every well-year

Map (right): mean simulated minus observed head per well, red = model too high, blue = too low, size = error. Points on the dashed 1:1 line would be perfect. Nearly all sit above it: the model water table is higher than the wells. Correlation is high only because both follow land-surface elevation, so it says little about skill; the bias is what matters.

One well through time

Caveats: a well is a point and the cell averages 4 km²; the model has one layer, so deep or confined wells cannot match; most wells were measured only after 2008.

Down the main stem: where the flow accumulates

Base run v17b, 2002–2003 mean. The model gains water at every reach; the river gauges show almost none. Points are USGS observations.

Where the excess comes from

Cause found and fixed. Rain-gauge files feeding the Sacramento foothills had no data for 2000–2012, so SWAT+ filled every day with its weather generator (about 1,020 mm/yr, peaking in August). Filling those days with gridMET cut Brantley's mean flow from 34.8 to 9.5 m³/s. In all, 79 of 129 stations used had more than 10% of days missing in 2000–2007.

Tributaries: observed against model

Mean 2002–2003, m³/s, log axis. Rio Hondo and Rio Peñasco were nearly dry at their gauges; the model runs about 1.5 m³/s in each. Channels matched to gauges by official drainage area.

Precipitation the model gave the foothill zone, and the resulting surface runoff.

Brantley mean by variant

What the tests found

1. Rain on oversized channels is the main source. QSWAT gave the Pecos channels widths of 350–1,400 m (2,074 km² of channel surface). Rain on that area is added to the flow and almost never evaporates, about 1.6 m³/s between Sumner and Brantley. Capping widths at 30 m removes 17% at Brantley.

2. The water-allocation crash is fixed. Any water_allocation.wro crashed on day 1 (an index used after being set to 0). A three-line guard is built as swatplus_wallo.exe and gives identical numbers to the stock exe on the control run.

3. Cell 13992 and PVACD pumping have no river effect with the stock exe. The groundwater flux never reaches routed flow, so head fixes and pumping changes match the base at every gauge. PVACD pumping matters (-0.59 m³/s at Brantley) only after the coupling fix.

4. The Hondo dams cannot be the main mechanism. The Diamond A gauge is above the dam and is already dry (0.01 observed against 1.72 modeled), so the loss is upstream. A 0.90 loss on Hondo and Peñasco stands in and gives the biggest single lever (-27% at Brantley).

5. Diversions and losses are real but supply-limited. Carlsbad and Fort Sumner canals and saltcedar ET remove water in proportion to what the simulated river can supply. Together with widths, v32a reaches 4.1 m³/s at Brantley.

6. Depth matters as much as width (v34). Channel width = 0.5717·A0.397 m and mean depth = 0.1225·A0.193 m (A = drainage area, km²), fitted to USGS channel measurements at 9 gauges (R² 0.62 width, 0.41 depth; p90 of measurements; never above the QSWAT value). QSWAT originals reach 1,396 m wide and 13.7 m deep, 9–27× and 3–15× the USGS values. Changing only depth on v32a takes Brantley from 4.12 to 2.03 m³/s. With processes plus corrected geometry Brantley and Red Bluff are within about 1.3× of observed, but Sumner falls to 0.4–0.5× (release too low) while Avalon (3.6–3.9×) and Orla (4.3–4.5×) stay high. Caveat: the curve rests on 9 points measured at gauges (stable narrow sections), and p90 is not bankfull. Screening on 2002–2003 (drought) overstates gains: v33 (v32a over 2000–2025) is still 4.2× at Brantley in 2010–2019 (13.98 vs 3.33), 3.4× in 2020–2025; v34b has not yet been run over 2000–2025.

Unverified assumptions.
  • Channel widths of 30–50 m (v34 curve from only 9 gauge points).
  • Riparian net ET of 0.5 m/yr over 4,687 ha, at a constant rate.
  • Tributary loss fractions of 0.90, set by gauges, not by a loss study.
  • Constant (non-seasonal) canal diversions.
  • Diverted and lost water leaves the model; it is not recharged to gwflow.
  • Arroyo ch 181 loss (v32b) is a pure assumption.

    Staged protocol

      Experiments so far

      Effect on mean flow at Brantley (2002–2003) unless noted. Observed: 2.35 m³/s.

      Routing defect (verified in the source). The groundwater–stream exchange computed by gwflow is written to ch_stor, but channel routing works on tot_stor and overwrites it, so aquifer flow, saturation excess and pumping never change river flow in this build. That is why the gwflow switches, the initial-head fix and streambed changes left flows unchanged. A one-line patch is under test (runs v24a–c).

      Ready to calibrate?

      Proposed acceptance criteria, in real units, monthly. Pick a run to see how far it is. Four-year runs give 24 months, so treat their statistics as rough.

      Bands: Sumner and Artesia ratio 0.8–1.25 and KGE ≥ 0.5; Brantley ratio 0.7–1.4, KGE ≥ 0.3, seasonal r ≥ 0.5; Avalon, Red Bluff and Orla ratio 0.5–2 and log-NSE ≥ 0; Hondo and Peñasco mean below 0.2 m³/s. KGE combines correlation, variability and bias; log-NSE weights low flows.

      Before automatic calibration

      Fix structurally first: the routing patch and re-test of pumping and aquifer levers; tributary delivery (infiltration, diversions, the Diamond A / Two Rivers dams); Brantley and Avalon release rules and the Carlsbad canal diversion; temperature-file gaps. Then calibrate a small set: delivery ratios for Hondo, Felix and Peñasco; CN2 by province; main-stem channel k; reservoir release fraction; riparian ET. Windows: warm-up 2000–2001, calibration 2002–2007, validation 2008–2012.

      Evapotranspiration: model against TerraClimate and SSEBop

      In this semi-arid basin evapotranspiration (ET) returns about 90% of precipitation to the air, so a small ET error is a large streamflow error. Simulated ET (HRU ET plus gwflow groundwater ET) is compared with two observation-based products: TerraClimate v1.1 (water-balance model, 4 km, monthly, 2000–2025) and USGS SSEBop (MODIS energy balance, 1 km, monthly, 2003–2025). Maps and tables are 2010–2019 means. The model runs wrote yearly output only, so model-product comparisons are annual; monthly and seasonal curves are the products alone.

      Mean annual ET, 2010–2019 (mm/yr), on a 0.1° grid

      Left: model (HRU ET + groundwater ET). Middle: the chosen product. Right: model minus product; green means the model evaporates more, brown means less. Cells hold the area-weighted mean of HRU centroids that fall inside them.

      Sub-regions, 2010–2019 means

      Boxes are approximate (latitude/longitude limits). Deficit is (product − model) ET as a flow: positive means the model is short of ET, which leaves extra water for runoff and recharge. r and KGE are for annual ET over the run's years (2002 onward).

      ET through time

      Seasonal cycle, 2010–2019 (mm/month)

      Products for the selected region, with TerraClimate precipitation. The model monthly ET will appear once run v37a_etmon (monthly basin and landscape-unit output) is finished.

      Evaporative index ET / P, by year

      Each source divided by its own precipitation (model: its station/gridMET rain; TerraClimate and SSEBop: TerraClimate rain). Above 1 means ET uses stored or imported water.

      Model ET partition, 2010–2019 (mm/yr)

      Canopy evaporation, plant transpiration, soil evaporation and groundwater ET, per region, chosen run. Reservoir and channel evaporation are given for the basin below the chart.

      Basin water balance, 2010–2019 (mm/yr)

      P − ET − Q. The model's residual is what feeds runoff and recharge; the products' residual is P(TerraClimate) − ET(product).

      Caveats

        Data: SWAT+ run outputs (), USGS daily discharge (NWIS), gridMET precipitation, NM OSE and USDA Census for context. Runs still in progress appear when this page is regenerated.
